subject: social
topic: False news travels faster than the truth
angle: False news spreads faster and further than truth because humans are more likely to share novel information that inspires fear, disgust, and surprise.
title: The Speed of Falsehood

hooks.text: Why does a lie reach you before the truth?
You think truth is faster. The evidence says it is not.
You share what surprises you. That is how lies win.
A thumb swipes. A lie travels.
False news travels faster than truth.

reveal.headline: Falsehoods diffuse farther and faster than truth.
reveal.body: False news spreads more broadly and deeper than the truth in every category of information. You are moving through a landscape where lies travel with more speed than facts.

explain.headline: Novelty drives the reach of lies.
explain.body: False news is more novel than true news. Humans are more likely to share information that is new or surprising. This behavior allows falsehoods to travel further than the truth.

matters.headline: Your attention is a target.
matters.body: That may be why your feed feels overwhelming. You are wired to notice the new and the surprising. Falsehoods exploit this biological tendency to reach you before the truth can.

example.headline: The scroll at 11 p.m.
example.body: You lie in bed. You swipe your thumb across the glass. A headline about a disaster appears. You share it before you check the source because it feels urgent and new. You have participated in the speed of a lie.

claims.text: Robots accelerated the spread of true and false news at the same rate.
claims.quote: Contrary to conventional wisdom, robots accelerated the spread of true and false news at the same rate, implying that false news spreads more than the truth because humans, not robots, are more likely to spread it.

claims.text: Participants were better at rating false news as false than at rating true news as true.
claims.quote: We found that people rated true news as more accurate than false news (Cohen’s d = 1.12 [1.01, 1.22]) and were better at rating false news as false than at rating true news as true (Cohen’s d = 0.32 [0.24, 0.39]).

claims.text: False news was more novel than true news.
claims.quote: We found that false news was more novel than true news, which suggests that people were more likely to share novel information.

claims.text: User interactions with false content rose steadily on both Facebook and Twitter through the end of 2016, but have since fallen sharply on Facebook while continuing to rise on Twitter.
claims.quote: User interactions with false content rose steadily on both Facebook and Twitter through the end of 2016. Since then, however, interactions with false content have fallen sharply on Facebook while continuing to rise on Twitter

claims.text: Falsehood diffused significantly farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly than the truth in all categories of information.
claims.quote: Falsehood diffused significantly farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly than the truth in all categories of information

claims.text: Participants who paused to explain why a headline was true or false indicated that they were less likely to share false information compared to control participants.
claims.quote: In an online experiment, participants who paused to explain why a headline was true or false indicated that they were less likely to share false information compared to control participants.

verdict: The evidence confirms that false news spreads more effectively than truth due to human behavior and novelty, though people are generally capable of discerning falsehoods.
caveat: While false news spreads more broadly, its relative magnitude on Facebook has declined since 2016 while continuing to rise on Twitter.
caption:
Falsehoods travel faster and further than the truth across all categories of information.

Research shows that false news is more novel, making humans more likely to share it. While people can often identify falsehoods, the speed of novelty gives lies a significant advantage. Note that while false news reach has fallen on Facebook since 2016, it continues to rise on Twitter.

Have you ever shared something only to find out it was false later?
